title: Conversion of life
hook: a vow to keep changing, little by little, every day

segments.voice: Yesterday, stabilitas, the Benedictine promise to stay with one community. Your line was stay. Where did you stay five minutes longer than you wanted to? Day one thousand one hundred fourteen.

Can you promise to change? Not to change one thing, by Friday, like a resolution on a sticky note. To keep changing, for the rest of your life, with no finish line. That's the strange second promise a Benedictine monk makes. Yesterday we heard the vow to stay. Sitting right beside it in the same chapter of the Rule is a vow that sounds like its opposite. Stay put, and keep moving. Same house, same brothers, same bells, and a heart that never settles into a groove. The Latin is two words, conversatio morum, and it doesn't go easily into English. You'll see conversion of life. Fidelity to the monastic way. Turning of habits. Today we take the first word: conversatio.

English versions often call it conversion of life. But this isn't the one dramatic turn, the light on the road to Damascus. It's turning as a way of living: a little more each day, the way a plant keeps leaning toward a window. The Rule never pretends anyone arrives. Near its end, Benedict calls the whole thing a little rule for beginners, written, he says, so that people can make a start. Then he points past it to scripture and the older teachers for anyone who wants more. A rule for a whole life, and its author files it under beginner. Paul says something like this in his letter to the Romans: "be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind." And to the Corinthians: "the inward man is renewed day by day." Day by day, not once. The Prologue of the Rule pictures where this leads. At first, it admits, the road is narrow and hard. But as a person goes on, the heart grows wider, and they run the way of God's commandments. It echoes a psalm: "I will run the way of thy commandments, when thou shalt enlarge my heart." So conversatio isn't guilt about not being finished. It's permission to never be finished. In this picture, nobody has to fix a whole life by Tuesday. The task is to begin again, today, and again tomorrow. Stability keeps you in the room. Conversatio keeps the room from going stale.

Here's the practice: change one small thing. Sit, and let the breath settle. Look at your day as if you were a stranger watching it. Somewhere in it is one tiny habit that's gone stale: the first thing you reach for in the morning, a tone you use with someone, a shortcut you always take. Pick one. Not the biggest. The smallest one you'd actually change. Decide what you'll do instead, just today. If you pray, you can offer that small turn to God. The bell holds the time.
Conversatio. The Benedictine promise to keep turning, a little each day, and never call yourself finished.
Your line: always beginning. Today, do the one small thing differently. If you forget, don't count it as failure. Start again. Day one thousand one hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns make the promise of conversatio morum together with stability and obedience, which the Rule pictures as a daily turning rather than one dramatic turn.

notes: Rule paraphrased. Chapter 58 for the triple promise; chapter 73 for 'a little rule for beginners' and the pointer to scripture and the Fathers; Prologue 48–49 for the narrow start and the enlarged heart running the way of the commandments. Check verse numbering.
Some manuscripts of the Rule read 'conversio morum' rather than 'conversatio morum'; left out of the script under the manuscript-claims rule. A Keeper may want it in the trapdoor.
'It doesn't go easily into English' and the sample renderings are a general description; confirm the renderings are fair.
No etymology of conversatio is given in the script (claims rule).
The Damascus road is a brief allusion (Acts 9), not quoted.
Editor pass: cut the stock 'Think of that' and the unsupported grammar claim that 'transformed' and 'renewing' are ongoing; 'it's borrowing a psalm' softened to 'it echoes a psalm'.

Audit pass: 'you only have to begin again' (narrator instructing the listener) now framed as the Rule's picture; Rule 73 'little rule for beginners', Prologue 48–49 and Romans 12:2, 2 Corinthians 4:16, Psalm 119:32 (exact KJV) rechecked.
